title: Beneath your feet
hook: a tree that fills your arms grows from a tiny shoot; a thousand-mile journey starts beneath your feet (Tao Te Ching 64)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was great things while small: the knot picked loose before it pulls tight. Your line was while it's small.

A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. It ends up on coffee mugs, desk posters and graduation cards, and it comes from chapter sixty-four of the Tao Te Ching. But the Chinese line doesn't quite say step. It says the journey begins beneath the feet. That small difference moves the starting line. It isn't out there, one stride away. It's under you, right now, wherever you're sitting.
screen: `A LINE FOR A COFFEE MUG.` → `NOT QUITE A STEP.` → `BENEATH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: First, three growing things. In James Legge's translation: "The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout." Then a tower of nine stories that rose from a heap of earth. Then the journey of a thousand li, a Chinese measure of distance. Each one is huge at the end and tiny at the start. Second, where the journey begins. The Chinese phrase is short: it begins below the foot. Legge renders it "commenced with a single step," which is how the mug got its line. The picture underneath is plainer: not a heroic first stride, just the ground under your shoes, the place you already are. Third, a warning near the end. People often ruin a thing when it's almost done, the chapter says, so be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and nothing will be spoiled. A long journey can fail on the last mile as easily as the first. Fourth, the chair you're in. The thing you've been meaning to start, the letter, the class, the conversation, the cleared-out closet, doesn't begin on some better morning, in some better mood. It begins from this chair, this kitchen, this hour, with whatever is already in reach. The tree didn't wait to be big. It was a sprout first, exactly where it stood.
screen: `A SPROUT, A HEAP, A JOURNEY.` · `IT STARTS BENEATH YOUR FEET.` · `CAREFUL AT THE END, TOO.` · then, large: `THE GROUND YOU'RE ON NOW.`

segments.voice: Rest both feet flat on the floor and feel them there: the weight, the ground pushing back. Name one thing you've been meaning to begin, keep it small, and ask what first piece can happen from exactly where you're sitting. When an answer comes, let your attention settle back into your feet.
Beneath your feet. In chapter sixty-four, the journey of a thousand li begins below the foot, right where you stand. Today's word.
Your line: beneath my feet. The starting line is already under you. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-four as a reminder to begin large things with the small step at hand, and to stay careful right through to the end.
